passage: When Jamal's café in Madrid closed after only eight months, Pablo heard the news from a friend and felt it: a quick, warm flicker of pleasure. Jamal had been so sure, so loud about "finally doing something real" while Pablo stayed in his office job. Pablo noticed the flicker and didn't like it. He said nothing in the group chat, where a couple of friends were already making jokes. Instead he walked home the long way and asked himself what the glee was about. The answer came slowly: he envied Jamal for trying at all. Pablo had been talking about his own bakery idea for four years. That night he texted Jamal: "Heard about the café. I'm really sorry. You were brave to try. Coffee this week?" Then he opened a blank page and wrote "bakery: first steps".

qa.a: Only eight months.

qa.q: What did Pablo realise the glee was really about?
qa.a: That he envied Jamal for trying at all, while Pablo had only been talking about his own bakery idea for four years.

qa.q: What choices did Pablo make after noticing the flicker?
qa.a: He stayed out of the group-chat jokes, sent Jamal a kind message, and then started writing first steps for his own bakery.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel receiving Pablo's text?
qa.a: Jamal would likely feel supported and less alone at a hard time, especially with others joking in the group.

passage: At the Thursday case meeting in the hospital seminar room, the senior consultant tore into Shankar's presentation: wrong dates, a missing scan. Shankar went red and apologised twice. Madhav, two rows back, felt something small and bright rise in his chest. Shankar had got the research fellowship Madhav had applied for. Madhav caught the feeling the way you catch your hand near a hot pan. In the residents' room afterwards, someone said, "Fellowship boy had a bad day," and waited for laughs. Madhav just refilled his water bottle. That night on the bus he asked himself what the brightness was really about. Not Shankar. His own stalled research, the paper he kept putting off. Next morning he found Shankar in the library. "I can help you check the scans for next week, if you want." Shankar looked surprised, then grateful.

qa.q: What was wrong with Shankar's presentation?
qa.a: Wrong dates and a missing scan.

qa.q: Why did Madhav feel something bright rise in his chest?
qa.a: Shankar had won the research fellowship Madhav had applied for, so seeing Shankar criticised brought a flash of pleasure.

qa.q: How did Madhav handle the moment in the residents' room, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He didn't laugh at the "Fellowship boy" line and just refilled his water bottle, keeping the glee from spreading.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt when Madhav offered to help?
qa.a: Surprised, then grateful, perhaps relieved to find a colleague on Shankar's side after a public embarrassment 🙏

grounding: A young doctor catches his glee at a rival's public criticism, does not join the joke, and traces it to his own stalled work.

passage:
Dear Omkar bhaiya,
I need to tell someone this, and you won't judge. Yesterday the civil services results came out, and Nikhil didn't make the list. For a second, I felt glad. Actually glad. You know how it's been, Papa always saying "Look at Nikhil, so focused" while I sit at my ordinary bank job.
I didn't say anything to anyone. I didn't send the "haha" the boys were sending in our group. I sat with the feeling instead, and I don't think it's about Nikhil at all. It's about wanting Papa to say something like that about me. That's mine to sort out, not Nikhil's failure to enjoy.
So I'm going to call Nikhil tonight, just to ask how he is. Wish me luck saying the right thing.
Hemant

qa.q: Where does Hemant work?
qa.a: At an ordinary bank job.

qa.q: What did Hemant realise the flash of gladness was really about?
qa.a: Wanting Papa to praise Hemant the way Papa praises Nikhil; it wasn't really about Nikhil at all.

qa.q: What does Hemant plan to do tonight, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: Call Nikhil just to ask how he is, keeping kindness for someone who is hurting instead of joining the "haha" messages.

qa.q: How might Nikhil feel if he saw the "haha" messages in the group?
qa.a: Nikhil would likely feel humiliated and alone on top of the disappointment of missing the list.

grounding: A young adult admits a flash of gladness at Nikhil's exam failure, keeps it private, and asks what the envy says about the writer's own life.

Dilnaz, you asked why I went quiet when everyone was laughing about Samira's fashion show. Okay, here's Zeenat being honest. When I saw the clips online, the models tripping on that wobbly ramp, the comments tearing her apart, I felt it. A little flash of glee. Samira, who told the whole batch at the reunion that she'd "made it" while I sat there in my export-office lanyard. Part of me went: good.
I didn't type anything. I didn't forward it. I just sat with it and asked myself, why does this feel good? And the answer was ugly but useful. I still sketch every night. I've never shown anyone. Samira at least tried.
So I sent her a message. "That ramp was a disaster, but the jackets were gorgeous." She replied with three hearts. And this weekend, I'm finally showing my sketches to someone. You.

qa.a: A message saying the ramp was a disaster, but the jackets were gorgeous.

qa.a: That it pointed to envy: Zeenat still sketches every night but has never shown anyone, while Samira at least tried.

qa.q: Which choice turned the glee into something useful?
qa.a: Not forwarding or posting, then asking what the envy pointed to, which led to a kind message and finally sharing the sketches.

qa.q: How might Samira feel on getting Zeenat's message amid the mocking comments?
qa.a: Samira would likely feel relieved and grateful to hear something kind and specific from an old batchmate.

passage: I'm Vaibhav, and I sit across from Yamini at the architecture firm. On Wednesday we heard that Tejal's big pitch, the one she'd been bragging about for weeks, had been rejected by the client. In the chat group, people started posting jokes. I saw Yamini read them. She smiled for a second, then put her phone face down. She said to me, not very loudly, "I felt glad just then. That's not great, is it? I think I'm jealous she got to lead it at all." She didn't post anything. After lunch she went over to Tejal's desk with two cups of tea. I don't know what they said. But later I saw Yamini open her own pitch folder, the one she'd never submitted, and start working on it again.

qa.q: What did Yamini take to Tejal's desk?
qa.a: Two cups of tea.

qa.q: What does Yamini putting her phone face down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she noticed her glee and chose not to join the jokes, stepping back from the feeling instead of feeding it.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yamini, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Naming her jealousy aloud; it led her to be kind to Tejal and to reopen her own pitch folder.

qa.q: How might Tejal have felt when Yamini came over with tea?
qa.a: Tejal might have felt comforted and a little surprised, since others were joking about the rejection in the group.

grounding: A colleague watches an adult notice her glee, not broadcast it, ask what the envy means and stay kind.
